Coax

KOHKS -- originally 16th-century slang, possibly related to 'cocker' ('to pamper'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To coax is to persuade someone gently and patiently to do something, especially something they're reluctant to do.

The camp counselor spent the better part of an hour trying to coax the homesick eight-year-old out of his tent.

Worked Example

The dentist spent extra time coaxing the terrified five-year-old into the chair with a sticker, a joke, and a lot of patience.

Notice coax always aims at one specific action or outcome -- getting the kitten out, getting the child into the chair -- through gentle, patient persistence, not through flattery for its own sake.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

urge: To urge is to press someone strongly and directly -- 'Apply now! Don't wait!' -- with the push right out in the open. To coax is the soft opposite: gentle, patient persuasion that eases a reluctant person toward what they resist, one kind word at a time.

prod: To prod is to keep nudging someone who is slow to act -- reminder after reminder, a poke in the ribs -- and it carries a note of impatience. To coax is patient and warm: instead of needling a person to hurry, you gently melt their reluctance away.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

compel: to force someone to do something

repel: to drive someone away or discourage them

Where it sits · how much effort winning them over takes — entice → coax → cajole

entice vs. coax: Entice is gentler than coax: a bakery's smell can entice people downstairs with no effort at all, while coaxing means patiently working on someone who resists.

cajole vs. coax: Cajole is stronger than coax: coaxing is gentle encouragement, but cajoling piles on flattery and persistence -- three phone calls' worth -- until the reluctant person finally gives in.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cokes-

root — cokes-: a fool (16th-century slang; the verb originally meant 'to make a fool of' or 'to pamper') (origin uncertain, possibly related to 'cocker')

Put it together

Put it together: Coax has a murky history, likely tracing back to old slang for making someone a fool, or for pampering them into doing what you want. Either way, the core idea has stayed remarkably consistent for centuries: winning someone over through gentle, patient persuasion rather than force.

Use the root in a new word: cocker

Use the root in a new word: cocker: Long ago, to 'cocker' a child meant to pamper and spoil them -- the same gentle, patient spirit behind coaxing someone today.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Coax aims at one specific, immediate goal -- getting someone to do a particular thing -- through gentle persistence. Compare Fawn, which showers someone with flattery and attention mainly to gain their general favor, without necessarily wanting one specific thing from them right now. You coax a toddler into the bath; you fawn over your boss hoping she'll simply like you.
